@notice The selector EBSI's Contracts Factory calls to initialize a
         proxy deployed against this implementation.
@inheritdoc ERC165

@title CertificateGovernance
 @notice Multisig governance layer over certificate status changes
         (component 10 of the Professional License Registry specification).
 @dev Component 10's independently verifiable proof that a status change was
      approved by a quorum before it was carried out. The certificates
      themselves live in CertificateRegistry, which a verifier reads
      without this contract; executed proposals set their standing there.
      - The contract never calls the back-office; it watches
        `ProposalExecuted` (or polls) instead, so neither depends on the
        other being reachable.
      - Nothing here identifies a holder: a proposal carries only the
        certificate's `statusKey`, so it is linkable to that record, not to a
        holder.
      Custom EBSI extension (component 10.0, subject to EBSI approval): EBSI
      deploys only pre-approved templates through its Smart Contracts
      Factory, which resolves a template's initializer via
      `getImplementationInitSelector` over ERC-165 (`supportsInterface`
      below) when supported. Reimplemented locally rather than depending on
      the factory's own code, since local/ebsi-mock is test/script-only and
      the prod build fails if anything under contracts/ imports it.
 @dev One contract for every TI of a TAO. The TAO sets each TI up
      (`addTi`); the contract keeps its rules and no status: whether a TI is
      active is read from the Trusted Issuers Registry and whether a key is
      valid from the DID Registry, each time, so revoking there is enough.
      Each TI has its own signers, cosigners, policies and proposal lifetime.
 @dev Version 2: rules are data. Each signer holds one role
      (component 10.2: pilot's A/B/C); a quorum counts distinct roles, not
      keys; each action/rule-change has a `Policy` (threshold, required and
      veto roles, timelock); a rule change waits out ADMIN's timelock
      unless vetoed (the key it removes can't veto its own removal); a
      signature only counts while its key is still a signer, and an expired
      proposal can no longer be signed or executed. Later came the V2
      commitment, typed roles, veto roles, timelock restart on regained
      quorum, retired keys, and the file split below.
 @dev Separation of duties in the back-office (component 1) and this
      multisig are NOT the same control (component 10.4): one is
      application-enforced, the other verifiable by a third party without
      trusting the certification body. They guard different threats.
 @dev Parts: governance/ holds the stateful modules, each with its own
      ERC-7201 namespace so a module can grow across an upgrade without
      moving another's storage: TiAccreditation (the EBSI registries, whether
      a TI is active), TiConfiguration (signers/roles/policies/TTL), Ballots
      (signing/quorum/timelock/veto/expiry), StatusProposals
      (suspend/revoke/reinstate, audit), RuleChanges
      (the contract's own rule changes). libraries/ holds stateless code:
      Roles (`Role`/`RoleSet`), Hashes, PolicyRules. interfaces/
      holds one interface per module, and IGovernanceTypes for what they
      share.

@title CertificateRegistry
 @notice Each certificate as the registry recorded it - the TI that issued
         it, when it is valid from and until - and its standing: valid,
         suspended or revoked.
 @dev The record is the only source of truth about a certificate,
      keyed by what every presentation discloses - the TI's DID and the
      credential's random id (`statusKey`) - replacing status lists entirely.
      The id reaches the chain only as a hash, and the certificate's number
      not at all. The record also keeps the hash of the signed
      credential, which ties it to that credential's content: a
      verifier compares it with the JWT it was shown. Registering and
      suspending at once take one signature (issuing is the body's own act;
      suspension is reversible, component 10.6); every other change
      (revocation, reinstatement, ordinary suspension) is a proposal that
      must reach quorum in CertificateGovernance, for a recorded certificate
      only.
      Who may sign is governance's question. What may happen to a certificate
      is this contract's, whatever governance asks: a revoked certificate
      stays revoked, an id is recorded once per TI, and a TI changes only its
      own certificates.

documentation.text:
@dev Adds the caller's signature; returns the signed roles and
      whether this completed the quorum. The timelock restarts
      whenever a lost quorum (key removed/replaced, stricter policy)
      is regained: to the contract that's a new decision, and 10.4
      gives every decision the full veto delay - otherwise a quorum
      lost at t0+47h and regained at t0+47.5h would be near-unopposable
      half an hour later. A signature is the only way a lost quorum
      comes back (a removed key stays retired, never revives). A
      policy relaxation is itself a rule-change decision and doesn't
      restart this timelock.

@dev Who may stop an open proposal: a veto-role key, or the proposer
      withdrawing their own. Withdrawal isn't a veto - it only stops
      what the same key started, so a compromised key gains nothing
      over simply not proposing, and the back-office needs it to close
      a rejected case on-chain regardless of who holds the veto.

@dev Signatures are aggregated on-chain, not collected off-chain and
      submitted together (10.4), so each is independently attributable
      and timestamped. A proposal for the same certificate past its TTL
      is expired here instead of blocking the new one. The reason travels
      as a salted commitment (`computeReasonHash`, 10.3): fixed once
      signed, unreadable on-chain; checked later via
      `verifyProposalReason`. Nothing is proposed for a revoked
      certificate; any other standing admits any action.

@dev Single-signer veto, not a quorum action: a timelock nobody can
      interrupt alone protects against neither a rash nor a
      compromised decision (10.4) - requiring a quorum to cancel would
      hand a 2-of-3 attacker the veto too. `vetoRoleMask` names which
      roles hold it; the proposer may always withdraw. Deliberately
      asymmetric: approving is hard, stopping is easy, since a wrongly
      executed revocation is terminal (component 1.1) but a wrongly
      cancelled proposal can be reopened.

documentation.text:
@dev Asks the Trusted Issuers Registry, on every call, whether the
      accreditation `attributeId` of `did` is live. In their latest
      revisions:
      1. the attribute exists and its type is `TI`, not `Revoked`;
      2. its `tao` is this contract's `taoDid`, so a TI accredited by
         another TAO is not active here;
      3. every parent, followed through `tao` and `parentAttributeId`,
         exists and is a `TAO`, up to a `RootTAO`. A path that reaches none
         within `MAX_TRUST_CHAIN_DEPTH` is not active.
      The path is walked here because the registry keeps a TI's type on
      its own attribute only: revoking a TAO leaves its TIs reading `TI`,
      and the check that would notice is internal to the registry.
      `attribData` is not read.

@dev Asks the DID Registry whether `account` holds a valid
      capabilityInvocation key of `did` right now, so a key that registry
      no longer shows stops counting at once. An unknown DID reverts in the
      registry; here it controls nothing.

documentation.text:
@title TiAccreditation
 @notice The EBSI registries this contract trusts, and the question it asks
         them: is this TI accredited right now? The registries are
         immutables of the implementation, given to its constructor: every
         proxy on the beacon reads them from the implementation's code, and
         no transaction changes them. On EBSI their addresses are fixed, so a
         key that could repoint them (the TAO's, if it were compromised)
         would only be a risk. Each network deploys its own implementation
         with its own registries; should EBSI ever move one, a new
         implementation version, which each proxy's owner opts into, carries
         the change.
@notice Roles are 1..8, so a set of them fits one byte.

@notice No timelock longer than this: a longer one is a typo that would
         freeze the TI, not a governance choice.
@notice No proposal lives longer than this.

@notice A proposal lives at least this much longer than the TI's
         longest timelock: time to collect the signatures, and then
         to execute. A shorter lifetime would let nothing pass, not
         even the rule change that lengthens it.

@dev A modifier that defines a protected reinitializer function that can be invoked at most once, and only if the
 contract hasn't been initialized to a greater version before. In its scope, `onlyInitializing` functions can be
 used to initialize parent contracts.
 A reinitializer may be used after the original initialization step. This is essential to configure modules that
 are added through upgrades and that require initialization.
 When `version` is 1, this modifier is similar to `initializer`, except that functions marked with `reinitializer`
 cannot be nested. If one is invoked in the context of another, execution will revert.
 Note that versions can jump in increments greater than 1; this implies that if multiple reinitializers coexist in
 a contract, executing them in the right order is up to the developer or operator.
 WARNING: Setting the version to 2**64 - 1 will prevent any future reinitialization.
 Emits an {Initialized} event.

documentation.text: @notice Sets whether to fall back to default RPC URLs when no URL is configured for a chain.

StdChains provides information about EVM compatible chains that can be used in scripts/tests.
 For each chain, the chain's name, chain ID, and a default RPC URL are provided. Chains are
 identified by their alias, which is the same as the alias in the `[rpc_endpoints]` section of
 the `foundry.toml` file. For best UX, ensure the alias in the `foundry.toml` file matches the
 alias used in this contract, which can be found as the first argument to the
 `_setChainWithDefaultRpcUrl` call in the `_initializeStdChains` function.
 There are two main ways to use this contract:
   1. Set a chain with `setChain(string memory chainAlias, ChainData memory chain)` or
      `setChain(string memory chainAlias, Chain memory chain)`
   2. Get a chain with `getChain(string memory chainAlias)` or `getChain(uint256 chainId)`.
 The first time either of those are used, chains are initialized with the default set of RPC URLs.
 This is done in `_initializeStdChains`, which uses `_setChainWithDefaultRpcUrl`. Defaults are recorded in
 `_defaultRpcUrls`.
 The `setChain` function is straightforward, and it simply saves off the given chain data.
 The `getChain` methods use `_getChainWithUpdatedRpcUrl` to return a chain. For example, let's say
 we want to retrieve the RPC URL for `mainnet`:
   - If you have specified data with `setChain`, it will return that.
   - If you have configured a mainnet RPC URL in `foundry.toml`, it will return the URL, provided it
     is valid (e.g. a URL is specified, or an environment variable is given and exists).
   - If neither of the above conditions is met, the default data is returned.
 Summarizing the above, the prioritization hierarchy is `setChain` -> `foundry.toml` -> environment variable -> defaults.

Adds the secp256k1 affine points `point1 = (pointX1, pointY1)` and
 `point2 = (pointX2, pointY2)`.
 The point at infinity is represented as `(0, 0)`.

Adds the secp256k1 projective points `point1 = (pointX1, pointY1, pointZ1)` and
 `point2 = (pointX2, pointY2, pointZ2)`.
 The point at infinity is accepted as `(0, y, 0)` for any non-zero `y` and returned as
 `(0, 1, 0)`. Any other result is normalized to `(x, y, 1)`.

Converts the secp256k1 affine point `(pointX, pointY)` to projective coordinates.
 The point at infinity is converted from `(0, 0)` to `(0, 1, 0)`.

Multiplies the secp256k1 affine point `(pointX, pointY)` by `scalar`.
 The scalar is reduced modulo the secp256k1 group order.
 The point at infinity is represented as `(0, 0)`.

Multiplies the secp256k1 projective point `(pointX, pointY, pointZ)` by `scalar`.
 The scalar is reduced modulo the secp256k1 group order.
 The point at infinity is accepted as `(0, y, 0)` for any non-zero `y` and returned as
 `(0, 1, 0)`. Any other result is normalized to `(x, y, 1)`.

Converts the secp256k1 projective point `(pointX, pointY, pointZ)` to affine coordinates.
 The point at infinity is converted from `(0, y, 0)` for any non-zero `y` to `(0, 0)`.

Signs data with a `Wallet`.
 Returns a compact signature (`r`, `vs`) as per EIP-2098, where `vs` encodes both the
 signature's `s` value, and the recovery id `v` in a single bytes32.
 This format reduces the signature size from 65 to 64 bytes.

Signs `digest` with `privateKey` using the secp256k1 curve.
 Returns a compact signature (`r`, `vs`) as per EIP-2098, where `vs` encodes both the
 signature's `s` value, and the recovery id `v` in a single bytes32.
 This format reduces the signature size from 65 to 64 bytes.

Signs `digest` with signer provided to script using the secp256k1 curve.
 Returns a compact signature (`r`, `vs`) as per EIP-2098, where `vs` encodes both the
 signature's `s` value, and the recovery id `v` in a single bytes32.
 This format reduces the signature size from 65 to 64 bytes.
 If `--sender` is provided, the signer with provided address is used, otherwise,
 if exactly one signer is provided to the script, that signer is used.
 Raises error if signer passed through `--sender` does not match any unlocked signers or
 if `--sender` is not provided and not exactly one signer is passed to the script.

Signs `digest` with signer provided to script using the secp256k1 curve.
 Returns a compact signature (`r`, `vs`) as per EIP-2098, where `vs` encodes both the
 signature's `s` value, and the recovery id `v` in a single bytes32.
 This format reduces the signature size from 65 to 64 bytes.
 Raises error if none of the signers passed into the script have provided address.

Signs a message with namespace using Ed25519.
 The signature covers namespace || message for domain separation.
 Returns a 64-byte Ed25519 signature.

Signs `digest` as a Tempo V2 keychain signature for `account` using a secp256k1 access key.
 Returns the encoded signature bytes accepted by `SignatureVerifier.verifyKeychain`.

Signs `digest` as a Tempo V2 keychain signature for `account` using a root or admin secp256k1 key.
 Returns the encoded signature bytes accepted by `SignatureVerifier.verifyKeychainAdmin`.
 The supplied `digest` should already be domain-separated with chain ID, contract address,
 and account address.
Signs `digest` with `privateKey` using the secp256r1 curve.

Signs `digest` with `privateKey` on the secp256k1 curve, using the given `nonce`
 as the raw ephemeral k value in ECDSA (instead of deriving it deterministically).
Signs data with a `Wallet`.
Signs `digest` with `privateKey` using the secp256k1 curve.

Signs `digest` with signer provided to script using the secp256k1 curve.
 If `--sender` is provided, the signer with provided address is used, otherwise,
 if exactly one signer is provided to the script, that signer is used.
 Raises error if signer passed through `--sender` does not match any unlocked signers or
 if `--sender` is not provided and not exactly one signer is passed to the script.

Registers a callback after exact mapping-element SSTOREs rooted at `rootSlot` in `target`'s effective storage account.
 The callback signature is `function(address account, bytes32 computedSlot, bytes32 rootSlot,
 bytes32[] keys, bytes32 oldValue, bytes32 newValue) external`; keys are raw words in
 root-to-leaf order. Only complete 64-byte Keccak chains observed after the latest mapping
 hook registration for `target` in the current top-level execution match; provenance is
 cleared between top-level executions. Resolution follows the complete chain to its terminal
 root and ignores registered intermediate hashes. Offsets, incomplete or unknown chains,
 hashes computed before registration or in an earlier top-level execution, and source layouts
 do not match. The contract that calls this cheatcode receives the callback. Registration
 persists across reverts and replaces the same target/root callback; callback state rolls back
 with its enclosing context, callback reverts propagate, and hooks are suppressed throughout
 callback subtrees. The callback must authenticate `msg.sender == address(vm)` to prevent
 external spoofing. Raw and mapping SSTORE hooks conflict per target, while multiple mapping
 roots may be registered.

Registers a callback invoked after each SLOAD against `target`'s effective storage account,
 including when its code runs by delegatecall.
 The callback must have the signature `function(address,bytes32,bytes32) external`.
 Registering another callback for the same target and access kind replaces it. Registration
 survives EVM reverts, while callback state follows the enclosing EVM context and rolls back
 with it. Callback reverts propagate through the storage operation. Hooks are suppressed in
 the callback and its entire call subtree. The callback must authenticate
 `msg.sender == address(vm)` to prevent external spoofing. Callback execution is hidden from
 mocks, expectations, log recording, and storage-access recording. It does not inherit
 staticness. The callback runs as an ordinary call frame and consumes one of the 1024
 protocol call-depth slots; a load at the maximum legal call depth can have its callback
 rejected as too deep, propagating as a failure of the load.

What the invariant fuzzer may do to two TIs of one contract: any of their
 keys (and keys that are not theirs) proposes, signs, executes, vetoes and
 changes the rules, the TAO changes their cosigners and moves them to
 another accreditation, both contracts are upgraded, while keys are revoked
 and restored in the DID Registry, a TI loses and regains its
 accreditation, and time passes.
 Every call may revert; the handler swallows it. What it keeps is a model
 of what the contract should hold (the "ghosts": each key's role, each
 certificate's standing, each finished proposal's state), built from
 what succeeded, and a list of the rules a successful call broke.
